---
title: "The terminal and bash, for GUI users"
subtitle: "If your career has been in Stata, Matlab, or RStudio, this is the missing ten minutes of context that makes Claude Code feel ordinary instead of intimidating."
---

Most economists I know have spent a career in **graphical** software: the
Stata window with its menus, Matlab's IDE, RStudio, Excel. None of those
require you to think about the terminal. So when Claude Code starts
typing things like `Rscript analysis.R` or `git status` in a black window,
it can feel like a different planet.

It isn't. The terminal is just the original way to talk to a computer:
type a command, hit Return, see the output. There are no menus and no
icons — just text in, text out. This page covers the **minimum** terminal
vocabulary you need to (a) follow what Claude Code is doing on your
behalf, and (b) type the few commands you'll actually need yourself.

::: {.callout-tip}
You do not need to *learn* the terminal to use Claude Code. You only need
to **read** what Claude does in it. Once you can read its output, you can
work confidently.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
**If you'd rather not work in a bare terminal at all**, see
[Using Claude Code inside VS Code](vscode.qmd). VS Code gives you a
graphical environment with an integrated terminal, so Claude Code edits
appear in a familiar diff view instead of a wall of text. Most colleagues
coming from RStudio/Stata/Matlab will find that route easier. You'll
still benefit from skimming this page — it explains what's happening in
the terminal pane at the bottom of VS Code.
:::

## What "the terminal" actually is

A terminal is just a window where you type a command and your computer
runs it. That's the whole concept.

- The window is called a **terminal emulator** (on a Mac, it's the app
  called *Terminal*; iTerm and Warp are popular alternatives).
- Inside that window, a small program called a **shell** is reading what
  you type and running it. On modern Macs the default shell is `zsh`. On
  Linux and on most Windows-WSL setups it's `bash`. The two are nearly
  identical for our purposes; people use the names interchangeably.
- Each line you type is a **command** — usually a program name, sometimes
  followed by **arguments** (what to run it on) and **flags** (options
  starting with `-` or `--`).

So when you see Claude Code run:

```bash
Rscript --vanilla analysis.R
```

That's three pieces: the program (`Rscript`), a flag (`--vanilla`,
meaning "don't load my personal R settings"), and the file to run
(`analysis.R`).

## How to open a terminal (Mac)

The fastest way:

1. Press `Cmd + Space` to open Spotlight.
2. Type `Terminal` and hit `Return`.
3. A small window with a blinking cursor appears.

You'll see something like:

```
yourname@your-mac ~ %
```

That's the **prompt**, telling you it's ready for a command. Type a
command, hit Return.

::: {.callout-note}
**Windows users:** install [WSL](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install)
and open "Ubuntu" from the Start menu. Inside, everything on this page
works identically.

**Linux users:** you already know how to open a terminal.
:::

## The seven commands you will see most often

These cover ~90% of what Claude Code does in the terminal and 100% of
what you'll ever need to type yourself.

| Command | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `pwd` | Print working directory — "where am I?" | `pwd` |
| `ls` | List files in the current directory | `ls` (or `ls -la` for details) |
| `cd` | Change directory — "move into this folder" | `cd ~/Desktop/papers` |
| `mkdir` | Make a new (empty) folder | `mkdir tables` |
| `cat` | Show a file's contents in the terminal | `cat README.md` |
| `cp` | Copy a file | `cp data.csv data_backup.csv` |
| `mv` | Move or rename a file | `mv old.do new.do` |

Two notes:

- The `~` symbol means "my home directory" — the one with `Desktop/`,
  `Documents/`, etc. So `cd ~/Desktop/papers` is unambiguous from
  anywhere.
- Hit `Tab` to autocomplete file and folder names. Type `cd ~/Des` then
  Tab → it fills in `~/Desktop/`. This is the single most useful keypress
  in the terminal.

## What "bash" really is, in one paragraph

A "bash script" (or "shell script") is just a plain-text file with a
list of these commands in it. When you "run" the script, the shell goes
through the file line by line and runs each command in order. That's
all. A `master.do` file is a Stata script. A `.bash` or `.sh` file is a
shell script. Same idea, different language.

Claude Code can read your shell scripts, write new ones, and run them.
It can also string together one-off commands without writing a script.
You don't need to learn shell scripting to use Claude Code — but knowing
it exists helps you read what Claude is doing.

## What Claude Code actually runs in your terminal

When you watch Claude Code work, you'll see it call out tools. The most
common one is `Bash`, which means "run this in the terminal". For
econ-research projects, the commands you'll see most are:

```bash
# Inspecting a project
ls
pwd
cat README.md
git status                  # what files have changed since last save
git diff paper.tex          # what specifically changed in paper.tex

# Running your code
Rscript scripts/01-clean.R              # run an R script
stata-mp -b master.do                   # run a Stata .do file in batch mode
python -m statsmodels analysis.py       # run a Python script
matlab -batch "run('main.m')"           # run a Matlab file
julia --project main.jl                 # run a Julia program

# Building a paper
latexmk -pdf paper.tex                  # compile a LaTeX document end-to-end

# Inspecting output
head output/table_3.tex                 # peek at the first lines of a file
wc -l data/clean.csv                    # count lines in a file
```

You don't need to memorize any of these. You just need to recognize that
when Claude says "I'll run the master script now" and you see a `Bash`
tool call with `stata-mp -b master.do`, that's the same thing you'd do
by clicking "Run" in Stata's window — Claude is just doing it in a way
that lets it read the output and decide what to do next.

## A quick note on `sed` — text editing from the command line

`sed` ("stream editor") is a small program that **edits text without
opening a file in an editor**. You will see it in inherited scripts; you
will occasionally see Claude Code reach for it when doing the same
mechanical change across many files at once.

It looks intimidating because the syntax is dense, but 95% of what
anyone uses `sed` for is one pattern: **find and replace**.

### The one pattern you'll see

```bash
sed 's/OLD/NEW/g' file.txt
```

In English: "in `file.txt`, substitute `NEW` for every occurrence of
`OLD`, and print the result." The `s` means *substitute*; the `g` means
*globally* (every match on each line, not just the first).

By default, `sed` prints the modified text to the terminal — your file
on disk is **not changed**. To actually save the change back, add `-i`
("in-place"):

```bash
sed -i 's/OLD/NEW/g' file.txt          # Linux / WSL
sed -i '' 's/OLD/NEW/g' file.txt       # macOS (note the empty '')
```

::: {.callout-warning}
**Mac vs. Linux foot-gun.** macOS uses BSD `sed`; Linux uses GNU `sed`.
The `-i` flag works differently on each. On macOS you must follow `-i`
with an empty string `''` (the "backup suffix"). On Linux you don't.
This bites everyone the first time. If you're following a script written
on a Linux machine and `sed -i` complains "extra characters at the end
of l command", that's the bug.
:::

### Examples relevant to econ work

Rename a variable across every `.do` file in a folder:

```bash
sed -i '' 's/wage_resid/wage_residual/g' *.do      # macOS
```

Strip carriage returns from a file your coauthor sent from Windows
(causes mysterious LaTeX errors):

```bash
sed -i '' 's/\r$//' paper.tex
```

Replace a hardcoded path in a script:

```bash
sed -i '' 's|/Users/coauthor/Dropbox|/Users/me/Dropbox|g' master.do
```

Note the `|` separator instead of `/` in the last example — `sed`
accepts any character as the separator, and `|` is much more readable
when the pattern itself contains slashes (like a file path).

### When Claude uses `sed` and when it doesn't

For editing your project files, Claude Code prefers its own `Edit` tool
— it shows you a clean diff per change and is harder to misuse. You'll
mostly see Claude reach for `sed` when:

- The same change applies to many files at once (e.g., rename a variable
  in 30 `.do` files).
- The edit is in a file Claude shouldn't keep "in memory" (a multi-GB
  log file, for example).
- A user has explicitly asked it to use the command line.

If you see Claude run `sed -i` against a file you care about, that
change is **not** going through the diff-review path you're used to.
Verify the result with `git diff` afterwards, or commit before letting
Claude run it so `git checkout .` is your undo button.

## Searching with `grep`

`grep` is the search tool. Give it a pattern and one or more files; it
prints the matching lines. Read-only — it never changes anything — so
it's safe to type freely.

The basic pattern:

```bash
grep "wage_resid" analysis.do
```

In English: "show me every line in `analysis.do` that contains
`wage_resid`."

The flags you'll actually use:

| Flag | What it does |
|---|---|
| `-r` | Recursive — search inside every file in a folder and its subfolders |
| `-n` | Show line numbers next to each match |
| `-i` | Case-insensitive |
| `-l` | List only the *filenames* that match (not the matching lines) |
| `-v` | Invert — show lines that **don't** match |
| `--include="*.do"` | Only look in files matching this pattern |

In practice, `grep -rn` is the workhorse — recursive search with line
numbers. Once you have it in your fingers, it replaces a lot of "where
did I define this variable" cmd-F'ing across files.

### Examples relevant to econ work

Find every place a variable is used across a project:

```bash
grep -rn "wage_resid" .
```

Find which `.do` files reference a particular dataset:

```bash
grep -rln "clean_data_v2.dta" --include="*.do" .
```

Find every TODO or FIXME comment a coauthor left in the code:

```bash
grep -rn -E "TODO|FIXME|XXX" .
```

Check whether a particular paper is cited in your manuscript:

```bash
grep -rn "smith2024" paper.tex appendix.tex
```

List every `.bib` entry by author surname (rough but fast):

```bash
grep "^@" references.bib | head      # entry types
grep "author = " references.bib | head
```

### When Claude uses `grep` and when it doesn't

Claude Code has a dedicated `Grep` tool that's faster and friendlier
than shelling out to `grep` (it uses `ripgrep` under the hood). You'll
usually see Claude use that instead. You'll see actual `grep` in scripts
written by humans, in old replication packages, and occasionally when
Claude is piping output through several commands at once.

Either way, the mental model is the same: **`grep` finds; it doesn't
change anything**. If you typed it and you don't like the result, type
something else. There's no recovery to do.

## Column work with `awk`

`awk` is the tool for **column-oriented text** — CSV files, log files,
TSVs, anything where you care about "the third whitespace-separated
field on each line." It's a tiny programming language in disguise. You
will use 5% of it; that 5% is genuinely useful.

By default, `awk` splits each line on whitespace and exposes the columns
as `$1`, `$2`, `$3`, … with `$0` being the whole line.

The basic pattern:

```bash
awk '{print $3}' file.txt          # print the 3rd column of every line
```

For CSVs (or any non-whitespace separator) use `-F`:

```bash
awk -F',' '{print $1, $4}' data.csv      # 1st and 4th comma-separated columns
```

### The four patterns that cover most use

```bash
# 1. Print specific columns
awk '{print $1, $5}' file.txt

# 2. Filter rows by a column condition
awk '$3 > 100' data.csv               # rows where column 3 > 100

# 3. Sum a column
awk '{sum += $2} END {print sum}' data.csv

# 4. Count rows matching a condition
awk '$3 == "treatment"' data.csv | wc -l
```

The `END {...}` block runs once after all lines are read — that's how
you accumulate totals or counts. There's also a `BEGIN {...}` block that
runs before any input.

### Examples relevant to econ work

Quickly peek at one column of a 10 GB CSV without loading it into R or
Stata:

```bash
awk -F',' '{print $7}' huge_admin_data.csv | head
```

Count distinct values in a column (rough but fast):

```bash
awk -F',' '{print $3}' data.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
```

Sanity-check a sum from a Stata table against the underlying data:

```bash
awk -F',' 'NR>1 {sum += $4} END {print "Mean wage:", sum/(NR-1)}' wages.csv
```

(The `NR>1` skips the header row; `NR` is awk's built-in row counter.)

Extract just the variable names from a Stata `describe` log:

```bash
awk '/^[a-z]/ {print $1}' describe.log
```

### Honest framing

`awk` is **rarely the right tool when you have R, Python, or Stata
already loaded**. Its real niche is the in-between moment: you want a
quick number from a file, and starting a full session in your stats
language is overkill. For that — and for one-liners that Claude Code
writes for you in a script — it's hard to beat.

Like `grep`, plain `awk` is read-only; it prints to the terminal. It
only modifies a file if you explicitly redirect output (`> newfile.txt`)
or chain it through `sed -i`.

## Other text tools you'll see in passing

You don't need to learn these, but recognize them when they go by:

- **`tr 'A' 'B'`** — character-by-character translation. Useful for
  uppercasing, stripping punctuation, normalizing line endings.
- **`cut -f3 -d','`** — extract a column from a delimited file. Like a
  one-trick `awk` for the "I just want column 3" case.
- **`sort` and `uniq`** — sort lines, then collapse duplicates. The
  `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` pattern (used in the awk example above)
  is the canonical "frequency table from a column" idiom.
- **`xargs`** — take a list of things from stdin and run a command on
  each. Common with `find ... | xargs grep ...`.

For all of these, the rule is the same: read what they do; let Claude
write them; verify the output.

## Safety: commands to never type without thinking

Most terminal commands are harmless. A few are not. Treat the following
the way you'd treat a power tool — fine when you mean to use it,
dangerous when you don't:

::: {.callout-warning}
**`rm -rf <folder>`** — recursively, forcefully deletes a folder and
everything inside it. **No trash, no undo.** Especially dangerous near
`~`, `/`, or `*` wildcards. Claude Code will prompt before doing this;
don't blanket-allow it.

**`sudo <anything>`** — runs the command as the system administrator. Almost
never necessary for econ-research workflows. If something is asking you
to `sudo`, slow down and figure out why. (The most common honest reason
is `sudo apt install` on Linux to install software.)

**`chmod 777 <file>`** — makes a file readable, writable, and executable
by everyone. The internet is full of "fix it with chmod 777" advice that
"fixes" the problem by making your machine less safe. Don't.

**`curl ... | bash`** or **`wget ... | sh`** — downloads code from the
internet and immediately runs it without you reading it. Even from
"trusted" sources, this is risky. Download first, read, then run.

**`git push --force`** to a shared branch — overwrites your coauthors'
work with no warning. If you're sharing a repo, never force-push without
talking to your coauthors first.

**`sed -i ...`** (or any in-place edit) without a git commit first —
silently rewrites the file with no diff and no undo. The fix is a
one-second habit: `git add -A && git commit -m "before sed"` before any
`sed -i` you didn't write yourself. See the [`sed`
section](#a-quick-note-on-sed-text-editing-from-the-command-line) above.
:::

The pattern: be suspicious whenever a command is **destructive**,
**privileged**, or **fetched from the internet and run sight-unseen**.
For everything else, the worst case is usually "type it again".

## When to let Claude drive vs. type yourself

A pragmatic rule of thumb:

- **Reading commands** (`ls`, `pwd`, `cat`, `git status`, `git diff`) —
  always fine for Claude to run automatically. They can't break anything.
- **Building / running code** (`Rscript`, `stata-mp -b`, `latexmk`) —
  fine for Claude to run, but watch for the failure mode where the script
  has side effects (writes files, sends an email, etc.). The first time
  you run a script under Claude, watch what it does.
- **Edits to your project files** — Claude does these via its `Edit` and
  `Write` tools, which show you a diff. Read the diff. Always.
- **Destructive shell commands** (`rm`, `mv` over an existing file,
  `git checkout` that discards work) — Claude prompts. Don't blanket-allow.
- **`git push`, `git push --force`, deploying anything** — type yourself,
  always. These are visible to other people. Make the decision consciously.

## A five-minute exercise

Open Terminal. Type each of these in order; press Return after each:

```bash
pwd
cd ~/Desktop
ls
mkdir terminal-test
cd terminal-test
echo "I survived the terminal" > note.txt
cat note.txt
cd ..
ls
```

You just: checked where you were, moved to your Desktop, listed the
contents, made a folder, moved into it, created a text file in it, read
the file, went back up one level, and listed the contents again. That is
the **entire** terminal vocabulary you need to start using Claude Code.

When you're done, you can clean up:

```bash
rm terminal-test/note.txt
rmdir terminal-test
```

(Note: `rmdir` only removes *empty* folders, so it's safer than `rm -rf`.)
